title: Parameter Initialization Strategies
description: Understand how neural network weights and biases are initialized, why initialization affects gradient flow and training stability, and how Xavier, He, orthogonal, and Transformer-specific initialization strategies are used in modern language models.
learningObjectives: Explain why neural network parameters require careful initialization.
Understand symmetry breaking and why identical initialization can prevent neurons from learning different features.
Derive the motivation behind variance-preserving initialization.
Distinguish Xavier and He initialization and identify when each is appropriate.
Understand orthogonal initialization and its relationship to signal propagation.
Describe initialization choices for embeddings, attention projections, and feed-forward layers in Transformers.
Implement and inspect common initialization strategies using PyTorch.
Recognize symptoms of poor initialization through activation and gradient statistics.

sections.title: 1. Why Parameter Initialization Matters
sections.content:
A neural network learns by adjusting trainable parameters such as weights and biases. Before training begins, these parameters need initial values. Initialization determines the starting point of optimization and influences the scale of activations, the magnitude of gradients, and the stability of early training.

Consider a linear layer: h = Wx + b. If every weight is initialized to zero, every neuron in the same layer receives identical parameters. During backpropagation, neurons with identical parameters and symmetric computation can receive identical gradients. They may therefore continue learning the same features instead of developing specialized representations.

Initialization also controls signal scale. If activations grow dramatically as they pass through many layers, numerical overflow or unstable gradients can occur. If activations shrink toward zero, useful information and gradients may become too small. A suitable initialization tries to preserve useful signal magnitudes across the network.

Initialization does not guarantee successful training. Architecture, normalization, optimizer settings, data quality, precision, and learning rate also matter. However, a poor initialization can make an otherwise reasonable training configuration difficult to optimize.

sections.title: 2. Parameters in a Neural Network
sections.content:
For a dense layer, the forward computation is z = Wx + b, followed by h = phi(z), where W is the weight matrix, b is the bias vector, x is the input, and phi is an activation function. For a batch of inputs, X can have shape [batch_size, input_features], and W can have shape [output_features, input_features]. The output has shape [batch_size, output_features].

The parameter count of a dense layer is output_features * input_features + output_features when one bias is used per output feature. For example, a layer mapping 768 features to 3072 features has 768 * 3072 weights and 3072 biases.

A Transformer contains several parameter groups: token embeddings, positional representations when learned, query/key/value projections, attention output projections, feed-forward matrices, normalization parameters, and possibly an output projection. Initialization policies can differ by parameter group because these components have different roles in signal propagation.
sections.example: If input_features = 4 and output_features = 3, W has shape [3, 4] and b has shape [3]. The layer contains 12 weights and 3 biases, for 15 trainable parameters.
sections.explanation: The weight matrix controls how input features are combined. Biases shift pre-activation values. Initialization sets the starting values of these tensors before optimization updates them.

sections.title: 3. Symmetry Breaking
sections.content:
Suppose a hidden layer contains 100 neurons and every incoming weight and bias is initialized to zero. Each neuron computes the same output for the same input. Under ordinary dense-layer training, the corresponding gradients remain identical, so the neurons do not naturally specialize into 100 different detectors.

Random initialization breaks this symmetry by assigning different values to different connections. Neurons can then produce different activations and receive different gradient signals. Randomness is not the only possible symmetry-breaking mechanism, but it is the standard practical approach.

A critical distinction is that zero initialization is not always bad. Initializing the bias vector to zero is commonly reasonable when the weight matrix is initialized appropriately. Initializing every weight in a hidden layer to zero is the problematic case. Output-layer biases and special parameters may also have intentionally chosen initial values.
sections.example: For two neurons with identical incoming weights, the same activation function, and identical biases, their outputs are identical for every input. If the gradients are also identical, gradient descent preserves that equality. Different initial weights allow the neurons to respond differently.
pitfalls: Do not confuse zero-initialized biases with zero-initialized weight matrices.
Random initialization should use a suitable scale; arbitrarily large random values can still destabilize training.
Reproducible experiments can use a fixed random seed without requiring all weights to be equal.

sections.title: 4. Variance and Signal Propagation
sections.content:
Consider a neuron z = sum from i=1 to n of w_i x_i, ignoring bias. Under simplified assumptions that inputs and weights are independent, centered, and have suitable finite variances, Var(z) is approximately n * Var(w) * Var(x). This approximation explains why the number of incoming connections matters when selecting the weight scale.

If Var(w) is too large, the variance of activations can grow with depth. If it is too small, the signal can shrink. Nonlinear activations alter the relationship, so the best scale depends partly on the activation function and architecture.

Backward propagation has a related problem. Gradients are multiplied by weight matrices and derivatives of activation functions. Their magnitudes may shrink or grow through many layers. Variance-aware initialization aims to improve both forward signal propagation and backward gradient flow, although one initialization cannot perfectly preserve every statistic in every architecture.
sections.formula: Var(z) approximately equals fan_in * Var(w) * Var(x)
sections.example: If fan_in = 256, Var(x) = 1, and Var(w) = 1/256, then the simplified approximation gives Var(z) approximately 1. This is a motivation for scaling weights inversely with the number of input connections.
sections.explanation: The formula relies on simplifying assumptions. Real networks contain nonlinearities, correlated activations, normalization, residual connections, and other effects that can change the observed variance.

sections.title: 5. Xavier or Glorot Initialization
sections.content:
Xavier initialization, also called Glorot initialization, balances fan-in and fan-out. Fan-in is the number of incoming connections to a unit, while fan-out is the number of outgoing connections. A common uniform form samples W from Uniform(-a, a), where a = sqrt(6 / (fan_in + fan_out)). The corresponding variance is 2 / (fan_in + fan_out).

A normal version commonly uses a standard deviation of sqrt(2 / (fan_in + fan_out)). These choices are designed to maintain a useful activation scale in networks where the activation function does not strongly suppress half of the signal, such as linear or tanh-like networks under suitable assumptions.

Xavier initialization is a starting point, not a universal rule. ReLU networks often use He initialization because ReLU sets negative pre-activations to zero and changes the variance relationship.
sections.example: For fan_in = 128 and fan_out = 256, Xavier uniform uses a = sqrt(6 / 384), approximately 0.125. Each weight is sampled within approximately [-0.125, 0.125].
sections.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(128, 256)
nn.init.xavier_uniform_(layer.weight)
nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)

print(layer.weight.shape)
print(layer.weight.var().item())
sections.explanation: The layer weight is initialized using the Xavier uniform distribution. Its bias is independently set to zero. PyTorch computes fan-in and fan-out from the weight tensor's shape.

sections.title: 6. He or Kaiming Initialization
sections.content:
He initialization, also called Kaiming initialization, is commonly used with ReLU-like activations. For a ReLU network, a standard variance choice is Var(W) = 2 / fan_in. The factor of two compensates approximately for the fact that ReLU removes negative activations under common symmetric assumptions.

For a normal distribution, the standard deviation is sqrt(2 / fan_in). For a uniform distribution with the same variance, the bounds are plus or minus sqrt(6 / fan_in).

The appropriate fan convention can depend on whether a tensor is used in the forward or transposed direction. Libraries provide options for selecting the assumed nonlinearity and fan mode. For leaky ReLU, the recommended gain depends on the negative slope.
sections.example: For fan_in = 512, the normal He initialization standard deviation is sqrt(2 / 512), which is approximately 0.0625.
sections.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(512, 256)
nn.init.kaiming_normal_(layer.weight, mode="fan_in", nonlinearity="relu")
nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)
pitfalls: Do not automatically use He initialization for every activation function.
For GELU and other smooth activations, architecture-specific choices may be used.
The initialization gain and fan convention should match the intended computation.

sections.title: 7. Orthogonal Initialization
sections.content:
An orthogonal matrix has orthonormal rows or columns, depending on its shape. In a square orthogonal matrix Q, Q transpose multiplied by Q equals the identity matrix. Multiplication by an orthogonal matrix preserves the Euclidean norm of a vector.

Orthogonal initialization constructs a weight matrix from an orthogonal or semi-orthogonal matrix, often with an optional gain factor. This can help control signal scaling in certain architectures, especially recurrent networks and deep transformations. It does not by itself solve all gradient-flow issues because nonlinearities, matrix dimensions, residual paths, and training dynamics still matter.

For rectangular matrices, orthogonality applies to the smaller dimension's orthonormal directions. The exact initialization behavior should be understood in relation to the tensor shape and how the matrix is used.
sections.formula: Q^T Q = I for a square orthogonal matrix Q
sections.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(128, 128, bias=False)
nn.init.orthogonal_(layer.weight)

identity = torch.eye(128)
error = (layer.weight.T @ layer.weight - identity).abs().max()
print(error.item())
sections.explanation: The code initializes the matrix orthogonally and measures its deviation from the identity after multiplying the transpose by the matrix. Floating-point arithmetic may produce a small nonzero error.

sections.title: 8. Initialization in Transformer Models
sections.content:
Transformers combine embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward networks, residual connections, and normalization. The best initialization therefore depends on how the complete block is arranged.

Token embeddings are often initialized with a small random distribution. Query, key, value, and output projection matrices are typically initialized using framework defaults or model-specific schemes. Feed-forward matrices also require scales appropriate to their dimensions and activations. LayerNorm or RMSNorm scale parameters are commonly initialized to one, with bias set to zero when the normalization includes a bias.

Residual branches deserve special attention. In a deep residual network, repeatedly adding branch outputs can increase the total activation scale. Some Transformer families scale selected output projections according to depth or use carefully designed initialization schemes. These methods seek stable signal propagation across many blocks.

There is no single initialization recipe used by every LLM. Published architectures may differ in embedding scaling, residual projection scaling, normalization placement, and output-head initialization. When reproducing a model, follow its documented implementation rather than applying a generic initialization to every parameter.
sections.example: A pre-normalization Transformer block may compute x_next = x + Attention(Norm(x)), followed by x_out = x_next + MLP(Norm(x_next)). The initialization of the attention and MLP branches influences how strongly each branch changes the residual stream at the start of training.
pitfalls: Avoid reinitializing pretrained weights when loading a checkpoint.
Do not assume all Transformer architectures use the same initialization.
Normalization parameters often have different initialization requirements from dense weights.
Initialization and residual scaling should be considered together.

sections.title: 9. Implementing Initialization in PyTorch
sections.explanation: The model applies He initialization to all linear layers and zeros their biases. This is a useful example for a ReLU-based MLP, but the final layer and other architectures may benefit from different choices. The printed standard deviations help inspect the resulting parameter scales.

sections.title: 10. Diagnosing Initialization Problems
sections.content:
Initialization problems can be investigated by measuring activation and gradient statistics across layers. Record the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and fraction of zero activations for representative batches. Also inspect gradient norms after backpropagation.

If activations grow by several orders of magnitude across layers, signal amplification may be occurring. If activations or gradients become extremely small, signal attenuation may be a problem. These patterns are clues, not definitive diagnoses; normalization, masking, saturation, and the data distribution can also affect the measurements.

A reliable experiment changes one factor at a time. Fix the random seed, use the same data and optimizer settings, compare initialization schemes, and track the initial loss and the first several hundred optimization steps. Check for non-finite values before assuming the problem is simply poor initialization.
sections.explanation: This diagnostic records activation statistics and checks whether values are finite after each layer. In a real experiment, compare these statistics across initialization schemes and several representative batches.

sections.title: 11. Choosing an Initialization Strategy
sections.content:
Use Xavier initialization as a common starting point for linear or tanh-like layers when its assumptions are appropriate. Use He initialization for many ReLU-based feed-forward networks. Consider orthogonal initialization when norm-preserving transformations are useful, especially in certain recurrent or deep linear settings. For Transformers, begin with the model's established initialization recipe.

The correct choice depends on the activation, fan-in and fan-out, layer topology, residual structure, normalization, and model depth. A default provided by a well-maintained framework may already be suitable for a baseline experiment. A custom initialization should be motivated by the architecture or an observed training problem.

Initialization experiments should compare more than final accuracy. Monitor training loss, gradient norms, convergence speed, activation distributions, numerical stability, and sensitivity to learning rate. Use repeated seeds when differences are small.

exercises.question: Why can initializing every weight in a hidden layer to zero prevent neurons from learning distinct features?
exercises.correctAnswer: Identical weights and biases make neurons produce identical outputs and typically receive identical gradients.
exercises.solution: The neurons begin in a symmetric state. During training, identical computation produces identical gradient updates, so the neurons remain equivalent. Randomly initialized weights break this symmetry. Zero biases are still commonly acceptable.

exercises.question: For a ReLU layer with fan_in = 200, calculate the standard deviation of normal He initialization.
exercises.solution: The standard deviation is sqrt(2 / fan_in) = sqrt(2 / 200) = sqrt(0.01) = 0.1.

exercises.question: For fan_in = 64 and fan_out = 192, calculate the variance of Xavier initialization.
Write PyTorch code to initialize a Linear layer with 256 input features and 128 output features using Xavier normal initialization and zero bias.
exercises.solution: Create layer = nn.Linear(256, 128), then call nn.init.xavier_normal_(layer.weight) and nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias). Ensure that the layer has a bias before attempting to initialize it.

exercises.question: A deep ReLU network produces increasingly large activation standard deviations across layers. Name two possible causes or interventions to investigate.
exercises.correctAnswer: Investigate weight initialization scale and residual or normalization behavior.
exercises.solution: Check whether the layers use an appropriate fan convention and He-style initialization. Inspect residual branches, normalization placement, activation distributions, and optimizer behavior. Compare controlled runs rather than assuming initialization is the only cause.

summary: Parameter initialization determines the starting scale and symmetry of neural network weights. Xavier initialization balances fan-in and fan-out, He initialization is commonly used for ReLU networks, and orthogonal initialization can preserve norms along selected directions. Transformer initialization must account for residual pathways, attention projections, embeddings, and normalization. Inspect activations and gradients, and follow architecture-specific recipes when reproducing an LLM.
